items.title: Risk Management for Business Continuity
items.abstract: Ensuring business continuity in critical cyber–physical infrastructures requires a holistic risk management approach that anticipates, quantifies, and controls complex cascading effects across interdependent services. This chapter presents the solution approach developed by the DYNABIC project, which pivots around RISKM4BC , a reusable methodology and supporting tools to manage risks that affect business continuity. The approach integrates: (i) a Bow-tie Smart Center that structures threats, barriers, and consequences and is augmented with information from Large Language Models (LLMs) to enrich scenario coverage and generate mitigation recommendations; (ii) predictive business process monitoring that forecasts the performance and risk of incident response workflows; and (iii) a cascading risk model that, based on Bayesian networks, quantifies interdependent risk exposure and updates it in near real time when new evidence arrives. The methodology is operationalized through traceable risk profiles and goal-oriented aggregation that align model outputs with business objectives, as well as through user-facing views that connect live evidence to decisions. A high-level architecture describes how these components interact with monitoring and digital-twin data to maintain a live risk picture for decision making of both human operators and automated responses. A running example from transportation infrastructure (by Ferrovial) illustrates how the methodology produces actionable risk alerts (e.g., congestion likelihood and business impact level), anticipates resolution timelines, and evaluates exposure to external dependencies (e.g., power or communications). We conclude the description of the approach with methodological advantages, lessons learned, and future extensions, including business-goal linking, automated incident reporting, and interactive what-if analysis.

items.title: SECOND LANGUAGE ACQUISITION IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE : A MULTI-PERSPECTIVE STUDY OF PERCEPTIONS
items.abstract: The acquisition of English as a second language (L2) is increasingly shaped by rapidly changing educational, social, technological, and digital environments, particularly in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). This study investigates the acquisition of English as a second language from the perspectives of students, teachers, and parents, with particular attention to the dynamic interaction of individual, familial, classroom, and technological factors. Guided by Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), the study conceptualizes English language acquisition as a dynamic and interconnected process that develops through the continuous interaction of multiple contextual and individual variables. A case-study research design was employed, and purposive sampling was used to select participants from Punjab, Pakistan. The study comparatively examines patterns of convergence and divergence across these three stakeholder perspectives to develop a multidimensional understanding of English L2 acquisition in the contemporary AI-mediated learning environment. Its practical implications extend to students, parents, teachers, educational institutions, policymakers, curriculum developers, and teacher-education programmes by informing the development of more responsive and technology-integrated approaches to English language learning. Furthermore, the findings may provide insights for AI and NLP developers, digital learning designers, social-media platforms, and digital content creators to develop linguistically accessible, learner-centred, and context-sensitive English-learning resources. Overall, the study seeks to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of how multiple stakeholders perceive and experience English L2 acquisition in an increasingly AI-driven educational landscape.

items.title: Security Monitoring and Multi-Concerns Resilience Analysis
items.abstract: Critical Infrastructures (CIs) are increasingly complex cyber-physical systems whose interdependencies expose societies to cascading failures triggered by cyber and physical threats. Traditional risk assessment methods and intrusion detection systems are insufficient to address rare, high-impact, and unforeseen attacks, highlighting the need for resilience-oriented approaches that extend beyond prevention. This chapter presents AWARE4BC, a framework developed within the DYNABIC initiative to enhance CI resilience and business continuity through Digital Twin–enabled services. AWARE4BC integrates continuous infrastructure monitoring, advanced attack and anomaly detection, and holistic resilience assessment based on runtime observations. It leverages heterogeneous data sources, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and semantically enriched threat indicators to support real-time situational awareness and evidence-based decision-making. Resilience is quantified through effectiveness and resilience curves capturing degradation, absorption, recovery, and adaptation across multiple concerns, including technical, economic, environmental, and social dimensions. The framework’s practicality is validated through a hackathon-based evaluation using a transportation use case, demonstrating its ability to detect both known and zero-day attacks and assess their cascading impacts. Results confirm the added value of combining security monitoring with resilience assessment. AWARE4BC offers a generic, modular approach applicable across CI domains, contributing to more robust and adaptive protection of essential services.

items.title: Sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers: Implications for biosafety and occupational vaccination – A systematic review with meta-analysis
items.abstract: This systematic review and meta -analysis estimated the prevalence of sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers (HWW) and evaluated hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination coverage and HBV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, SciELO, the Virtual Health Library, the CAPES Periodicals Portal, and Google Scholar were searched through 19 May 2026. Twenty-two studies involving approximately 9,000 HWW and 1,722 sharps injuries were included. Random-effects meta -analyses used logit transformation and restricted maximum likelihood estimation. The pooled prevalence of sharps injuries was 34.1% (95% CI, 22.8–47.5%), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.9%). HBV vaccination coverage was 31.1% (95% CI, 8.2–68.3%) and was not associated with sharps injury prevalence (β = 0.338; p = 0.544). Pooled HBV and HCV prevalence estimates were 2.3% (95% CI, 0.3–15.4%) and 3.36% (95% CI, 1.17–9.23%), respectively. No HCV seroconversion was reported in follow-up studies. Approximately one-third of HWW experienced sharps injuries, highlighting the need to strengthen waste segregation, personal protective equipment use, biosafety training, HBV vaccination, and occupational surveillance to improve worker safety and reduce preventable blood-borne infections.

items.title: Social Risk Management of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: With the rapid uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, academic risks need to be viewed as not only technical issues but as socio-institutional harms that impact equity, trust, and accountability. The methodology used for this study is a conceptual literature review and qualitative synthesis of existing academic research. This study tackles the problem existing in the literature, which is unstructured definitions, by synthesizing the literature to create a complete conceptual framework for Social Risk Management (SRM). The proposed framework places SRM in a unique role, serving as the institutional interface between the introduction of AI and social outcomes, with the role of a mediator and moderator between the raw technical inputs and the negative effects of AI on society. There are four main operational pillars of SRM identified in the synthesis. This study also adds the competency of SRM as a core competency of governance, not only for its ethical dimension but also for being a proactive competency. Moreover, it offers a clear research program for future empirical studies, detailing potential ways to measure SRM and to investigate its differences in various application areas of universities, such as admissions, financial aid, tutoring, and even assessment.

items.title: Standardization, Framing, and Governance Absence: A Systematic Review of Human-AI Relationships Across Engineering, Ethics, and Policy
items.abstract: Abstract AI systems increasingly serve as social partners, companions, and romantic partners, yet governance remains fragmented, reactive, and split between clinical applications and anthropomorphic deception. Current Canadian AI regulation (PIPEDA and the un-proclaimed AIDA) addresses privacy and market access only, while Character.AI and a growing list of anthropomorphic-chatbot suicide cases point directly to the product-liability question that no Canadian instrument answers. This gap illustrates the regulatory break that motivates this paper. In the physcial world, the ethics → policy → engineering loop (EPE loop) works as a mutually protective cycle in which ethics specifies the values a system must serve, engineering builds mechanisms that support them, and policy verifies and enforces them, so that companies and stakeholders share benefits from a standardized technique world. Virtual AI services and products, however, do not inherit that protection. Their values are relational, their mechanisms conversational, and their harms uncodified, so the EPE loop does not close. This systematic review of 169 studies examines where the loop breaks. This systematic review examines how engineering, ethics, and policy shape human-AI relationships between 2022-2026 and identifies challenges and opportunities at their intersections. Following PRISMA 2020, seven databases yielded 395 records; 169 studies met inclusion criteria. Reflexive Thematic Analysis and K-means clustering synthesized our findings. We identify three distinct clusters. The empirical group (n = 30) is characterized by empirical research that documents deception and vulnerability but lacks governance support, producing a regulatory gap. The anthropomorphism group (n = 83) focuses on engagement and safety, and is characterized by the highest standardization gaps that is mostly implicit stated, meaning researchers name the harms but never specify the technique standards against which those harms would be measured. The clinical group (n = 56) shows strong policy engagement but the largest conceptual framing gap, and its high principle-to-practice gap indicates that the gap becomes visible precisely because its principles are codified, yet the cluster lacks broad conceptual exploration of additional missing values such as relational and communicative harms. We show that the three governance failures are three skipped Value-Senstive-Design (VSD) obligations: technical (Cluster 1), conceptual (Cluster 2), and empirical-to-instrument (Cluster 0). We propose a research agenda that closes each gap. For anthropomorphic AI, technique solutions developed into technical standards; for highly regulated domains, broader conceptual maps of the values they have not yet admitted; and, across all three clusters, stakeholder-anchored empirical work under VSD framework. We further argue that VSD values are not exhausted by design values but include ethical values and, potentially, policy values, which is what allows the EPE loop to rotate again. So that the next anthropomorphic-AI suicide case could be decided by a standard rather than by a motion to dismiss.

items.title: Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. We analyzed these behaviors in 880 substantive turns from 112 secondary-school students completing open-ended mathematical-modeling practice with a general-purpose LLM (Mistral). Overall, students showed limited observable epistemic proactivity: their interactions were strongly request-dominated, with planning, monitoring, and evaluation relatively rare, although low-quality AI responses elicited more explicit evaluation. Temporal analyses qualified this picture: explicit SRL-related moves increased modestly over the chat, but help-seeking strategies became less understanding-oriented. Crucially, these temporal trajectories in help-seeking strategies predicted their post-test performance without AI beyond pre-test and aggregate patterns: students whose requests became more understanding-oriented performed better once AI assistance was removed. Thus, while students had a limited epistemic proactivity overall, its temporal development still was a critical predictor of post-test performance without AI. These results underscore the importance of examining the temporal organization of epistemic proactivity, rather than isolated prompt types, for understanding AI-supported learning. We release our fully-anonymized dataset publicly in an OSF repository.

items.abstract: The major objective of this lecture is to summarize the evolution of computational ophthalmology over the past 2 decades through the scientific advances that have transformed ophthalmic research. Topics include the emergence of computational ophthalmology, the role of big data in scientific discovery, the application of machine learning to ophthalmic imaging, and the development of artificial intelligence (AI)-ready data ecosystems. The lecture concludes by exploring the next frontier in computational ophthalmology, highlighting foundation models and agentic AI as emerging approaches with the potential to accelerate scientific discovery, and improve clinical care are discussed. items.title: The Algorithmic Co-Thinker: A Generative AI Framework for Persona-Aware Computational Mathematics
items.abstract: The integration of Computational Thinking (CT) into mathematics education frequently encounters challenges within Digital Mathematics Learning Environments (DMLEs), which often adopt static, one-size-fits-all approaches that fail to adequately support learner diversity. While prior studies have identified distinct learner personas—such as the Frustrated Perfectionist and the Conceptually Stalled Learner—a critical barrier remains in scaling personalized, real-time pedagogical support. This study proposes a novel framework utilizing Generative AI (GenAI) to transform DMLEs into dynamic “co-thinkers.” Employing a two-phase design-based research methodology, we first empirically validated a four-persona typology through qualitative analysis and quantitative behavioral signatures. Subsequently, we developed and expert-validated a conceptual GenAI scaffolding prototype, comprising structured prompt templates engineered to deliver metacognitive and affective support tailored to individual persona needs. Preliminary expert validation confirms pedagogical soundness and highlights key ethical considerations. The paper presents this integrative framework alongside a detailed discussion of its design principles, operative AI cycle, and embedded ethical safeguards, positioning persona-aware AI as a transformative, yet responsible, pathway for computational mathematics education.

items.title: The DYNABIC Approach and Architecture
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the DYNABIC framework, a comprehensive and adaptive cybersecurity solution designed to enhance the resilience of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) in the face of evolving cyber-physical threats. The framework integrates advanced technologies such as digital twins, artificial intelligence, and cyber threat intelligence to enable real-time threat detection, simulation, and response. At its core, DYNABIC employs a bidirectionally synchronized digital twin to model and simulate cyber-physical systems, supporting dynamic risk mitigation and adaptive response strategies across the four phases of the resilience cycle: Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, and Adapt. The architecture is modular and scalable, fostering collaboration among CIs and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs). It includes key components such as MADT4BC, SOAR4BC, RISKM4BC, SIM4BC, AWARE4BC, and CTI4BC, which collectively support real-time monitoring, risk assessment, incident simulation, automated response, and threat intelligence sharing. The framework also incorporates a human-in-the-loop interface (AVATAR4BC) to enhance situational awareness and decision-making.

items.title: The Effect of Transformational Leadership and Employee Engagement on Employee Performance in the Service Industry
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of transformational leadership and employee engagement on employee performance within the service industry. As organizations in this sector increasingly compete on service quality, customer satisfaction, and operational efficiency, understanding the human factors that drive employee performance has become a strategic priority for management. Transformational leadership, characterized by idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, is theorized to enhance employees' motivation, commitment, and willingness to exceed expected job requirements. Similarly, employee engagement, reflecting the degree of vigor, dedication, and absorption employees exhibit toward their work, is considered a critical psychological state that translates leadership influence into tangible performance outcomes. This research employs a quantitative approach using a survey method distributed to employees working in service-based organizations. Data were collected through structured questionnaires measuring transformational leadership, employee engagement, and employee performance, and were analyzed using multiple regression analysis to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings reveal that both transformational leadership and employee engagement have a positive and significant effect on employee performance, whether tested partially or simultaneously. Transformational leadership was found to strengthen employees' sense of purpose and trust in their leaders, which in turn fosters higher engagement and, consequently, improved performance outcomes. Employee engagement was also identified as a key mediating mechanism linking leadership behavior to performance results. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on leadership and human resource management by providing empirical evidence from the service industry context, where interpersonal interaction and employee behavior directly affect service delivery quality.
